# Tuesday agenda

<div class="result-band"><strong>Focus:</strong> choose evidence that fits the question and explain what it supports. Companion notebook: <strong>W11_RMDS_Inference_Lab.ipynb</strong></div>

<div class="agenda-line"><span class="n">1</span>Comparing two variables with real evidence</div>
<div class="agenda-line"><span class="n">2</span>Sampling variation and confidence intervals</div>
<div class="agenda-line"><span class="n">3</span>Tests, null models, and p-values</div>
<div class="agenda-line"><span class="n">4</span>Effect size and substantive importance</div>
<div class="agenda-line"><span class="n">5</span>Evidence choices for research questions</div>
<div class="agenda-line"><span class="n">6</span>Preparation for Thursday</div>

???
Two 75-minute meetings for 12 students. Tuesday: opening5 + comparisons12 + sampling/CI24 + tests12 + effect/importance10 + evidence choice9 + preparation3 =75. Thursday: source10 + estimate10 + sampling10 + bootstrap12 + permutation10 + choice application10 + reporting/project10 + save3 =75. Dividers are included. Real NSW experimental subset:185 training and260 controls. Files do not reconstruct original assignment blocks or the full protocol; independent-participant inference is a teaching approximation. Appendix and paired extensions are optional. No new grading weights or deadlines. Allow 1 minute for the agenda.


---

class: balanced

# Description and inference

<div class="split">
  <div class="split-panel"><h2>Description</h2><p>A graph or table summarises the records you observed.</p></div>
  <div class="split-panel alt"><h2>Inference</h2><p>The analysis asks what those records support about a defined target under explicit assumptions.</p></div>
</div>

<div class="activity-box"><strong>PAIR DISCUSSION · 3 MIN</strong><br>If two groups have different average earnings, what else must you know before claiming that a programme worked?</div>

<div class="student-note"><strong>Key distinction:</strong> description stays with the observed records; inference connects those records to a target beyond the sample.</div>

???
Opening remaining4 minutes: framing1, pairs2, report1. Ask for design, selection, measurement, sample size, variability and dependence. Random assignment supports a comparison; random sampling addresses representation. An observed gap alone does not establish a causal effect.


---

# 1. Bivariate questions have different forms

<div class="evidence-list">
  <div class="evidence-row"><strong>Group + number</strong><span>Training group and earnings</span><span>Group summaries and distributions</span></div>
  <div class="evidence-row"><strong>Number + number</strong><span>Earnings in two baseline years</span><span>Scatterplot and association measure</span></div>
  <div class="evidence-row"><strong>Group + binary</strong><span>Training group and positive earnings</span><span>Counts, proportions, and percentage-point gap</span></div>
</div>

<div class="result-band">Variable types help choose the comparison. Study design determines the claim.</div>

<div class="student-note"><strong>First step:</strong> name the type of each variable. That decision narrows the sensible summaries, plots, and methods.</div>

???
3 minutes. Bivariate means examining two variables together. A binary outcome is a two-category variable. Do not choose a test before checking units, independence and the intended quantity.


---

class: balanced

# Study question and observed earnings

<div class="split wide-left">
  <div class="split-panel">
    <h2>National Supported Work study</h2>
    <p><strong>Primary question:</strong> How do mean 1978 real earnings differ between the training and control groups?</p>
    <p>The analysis uses the source-dollar scale. The sample does not represent all workers or current monetary values.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="split-panel alt">
    <h2>Observed participants</h2>
    <p><strong>185</strong> training participants</p>
    <p><strong>260</strong> controls</p>
    <p>Zeros are valid earnings observations, not missing values.</p>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="stat-strip">
  <div class="stat"><strong>6,349</strong>Training mean</div>
  <div class="stat"><strong>4,555</strong>Control mean</div>
  <div class="stat"><strong>1,794</strong>Observed mean gap</div>
  <div class="stat"><strong>445</strong>Total observed N</div>
</div>

<div class="student-note">The 1,794-dollar gap is an estimate from this sample. Its uncertainty and the study design determine how far the claim can extend.</div>

???
6 minutes. Use the experimental files, not the CPS/PSID comparison groups. The authors selected this subset using pre-intervention information. Preserve source-dollar units because the data page does not specify a price base. Public records do not reconstruct the full assignment protocol or attrition history. Group details: control median3139 and SD5484; training median4232 and SD7867. Means exceed medians, indicating skew and variability. No deletion or winsorization. The primary quantity is the difference in means.


---

class: small

# The distributions need inspection

<div class="plot"><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="The distributions need inspection" /></div>

.caption[Which features could affect a mean comparison? Discuss for one minute.]

<div class="student-note"><strong>How to read:</strong> the ECDF shows the share at or below each earnings value; the boxplot highlights centre, spread, and unusual observations.</div>

???
3 minutes including a one-minute pair observation. ECDF means share at or below a value. Many zeros and high values matter for means. A boxplot flag does not establish an error. Comparisons block:3+3+3+3=12 minutes.


---

class: inverse, center, middle

# 2. Sampling variation and confidence intervals



<div class="section-subtitle">The next question is why a reasonable estimate changes from sample to sample and how an interval expresses that uncertainty.</div>

???
Section transition included within its block timing.


---

class: balanced

# Standard deviation and standard error

<div class="split">
  <div class="split-panel"><h2>SD · individuals</h2><p>Standard deviation describes how much individual outcomes vary.</p></div>
  <div class="split-panel alt"><h2>SE · estimates</h2><p>Standard error describes how an estimator varies across repeated samples under its model.</p></div>
</div>

<div class="definition"><strong>Independent-group mean contrast:</strong> SE = sqrt(SD₁² / n₁ + SD₀² / n₀)</div>

<div class="result-band">More observations can reduce SE without making individuals more alike.</div>

<div class="student-note"><strong>Memory aid:</strong> SD describes variation among people; SE describes the precision of an estimate.</div>

???
2 minutes. Welch permits unequal variances but still needs independent units and an adequate mean-approximation. The SDs in previous table are not standard errors. Do not require students to memorize Welch degrees of freedom.


---

class: small

# A teaching experiment shows sampling variation

<div class="plot"><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="A teaching experiment shows sampling variation" /></div>

.caption[Simulated draws from the real control earnings used as a known reference distribution.]

<div class="student-note">The narrower distribution for n = 100 means that larger samples produce more stable means in this reference world.</div>

???
3 minutes. The fixed empirical control distribution is the known teaching reference world. Draw independent samples with replacement. The spread of means is about1096 at n25 and536 at n100. These are resamples, not new observed participants or a reconstruction of the actual population.


---

class: balanced

# Sampling challenge — pairs, 3 minutes

The reference distribution stays the same.

Sample size increases from **25 to 100**.

1. Predict the change in the spread of sample means.
2. Does increasing the sample remove systematic selection bias?
3. Are 2,000 simulated samples the same as observing 2,000 new participants?

<div class="student-note">Changing sample size changes random sampling variation. It does not automatically correct biased selection or poor measurement.</div>

???
2 minutes in pairs and1 minute for discussion. Quadrupling n roughly halves SE. Larger samples do not remove selection bias. Increasing replication count does not increase the original sample size.


---

class: balanced

# Confidence intervals concern estimates

<div class="definition"><strong>Interval = estimate ± critical value × SE</strong></div>

<div class="split">
  <div class="split-panel"><h2>Repeated procedure</h2><p>Under its assumptions, a 95% procedure covers the fixed target in approximately 95% of repeated studies.</p></div>
  <div class="split-panel alt"><h2>Observed interval</h2><p>Report the range, target, method, and assumptions for the interval you calculated.</p></div>
</div>

<div class="caution">The interval does not describe individual earnings and does not assign a probability to the fixed target.</div>

<div class="student-note">A 95% confidence level describes the long-run success rate of the method, not the probability that this one fixed interval is correct.</div>

???
3 minutes. Frequentist repeated-procedure interpretation. The target and appropriate repeated-study model must be specified. Unknown true target is fixed; observed interval varies with data before observation. Approximate methods need not attain exact nominal coverage.


---

class: small

# The real mean difference with uncertainty

<div class="plot"><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="The real mean difference with uncertainty" /></div>

.caption[Estimate: 1,794. Approximate 95% Welch interval: 474 to 3,115 source dollars.]

<div class="student-note"><strong>How to read:</strong> the dot is the estimated mean gap; the horizontal line shows values reasonably compatible with the data and model.</div>

???
3 minutes. Welch difference1794.34, SE671, df307, t2.674 and p.00789. Interval474.01–3114.67. Keep the study context and model assumptions explicit. A mean contrast does not state individual treatment effects or programme net benefits.


---

class: small

# Repeated intervals illustrate coverage

<div class="plot"><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Repeated intervals illustrate coverage" /></div>

.caption[The dashed line is the known mean of the teaching reference distribution.]

<div class="student-note">Each horizontal line comes from a new simulated sample. Most cross the known target, while a small number miss it.</div>

???
3 minutes. Display40 of400 simulated intervals from size80 samples of the empirical control distribution. This seed happens to give95% coverage across400, but another realization or method can differ. In a real study the target is unknown; this teaching world makes coverage visible.


---

class: balanced

# Interval interpretation — pairs, 4 minutes

Which claims follow from the earnings interval?

A. Most participants gained between 474 and 3,115 dollars.

B. The estimated mean contrast is positive, with substantial uncertainty about its size.

C. The programme is proven worthwhile in every country.

Explain your choice and repair one incorrect claim.

<div class="student-note">Keep the target clear: this interval concerns a group mean difference, not the earnings change of every participant.</div>

???
2 minutes in pairs and2 for debrief. B is defensible within the study and assumptions. A confuses a mean-contrast interval with individual gains. C invents external validity and benefit-cost evidence.


---

class: small

# Bootstrap resampling estimates uncertainty

<div class="plot"><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Bootstrap resampling estimates uncertainty" /></div>

.caption[Resample people within each group with replacement. The contrast varies around the observed estimate.]

<div class="student-note">Bootstrap samples are generated from the observed groups, so the distribution remains centred near the observed contrast rather than zero.</div>

???
3 minutes. The default bootstrap uses5000 replications with seed1103, resampling within arms of size185 and260. Percentile limits are approximately522–3186. This is an independent-within-group approximation. The distribution is not a zero-null reference. Sampling/CI block:2+3+3+3+3+3+4+3=24 minutes.


---

class: inverse, center, middle

# 3. Tests, null models and p-values



<div class="section-subtitle">Testing asks how unusual the observed statistic would be if a specified null model generated the data.</div>

???
Section transition included within its block timing.


---

class: balanced

# Hypothesis test and p-value

<div class="split">
  <div class="split-panel">
    <h2>The question</h2>
    <p><strong>Null:</strong> the target mean contrast equals zero.</p>
    <p><strong>Alternative:</strong> the contrast differs from zero.</p>
    <p>The two-sided Welch test compares the standardized observed gap with its null reference.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="split-panel alt">
    <h2>The evidence</h2>
    <p><strong>Two-sided p = 0.0079</strong></p>
    <p>Under the null model, this is the probability of a statistic at least as extreme as the observed one.</p>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="caution">The p-value does not give the probability that the null is true, the size or importance of the contrast, or proof that bias is absent.</div>

<div class="student-note">A small p-value describes tension between the data and the null model. It does not by itself establish causality or practical value.</div>

???
6 minutes. Specify the outcome, direction, test, and assumptions before seeing a preferred result. The null concerns the target mean contrast, not every individual effect. Explain p=.0079 as a null-model tail probability, not the probability that the null is true or that the result occurred by chance. A threshold is not a scientific truth boundary. Randomized-origin evidence and representative sampling remain different issues.


---

class: small

# A null reference uses a different operation

<div class="plot"><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="A null reference uses a different operation" /></div>

.caption[Bootstrap: uncertainty around the contrast. Shuffled labels: an exchangeable-label null reference.]

<div class="student-note"><strong>Compare the centres:</strong> bootstrap contrasts cluster near the estimate; shuffled-label contrasts cluster near the null value of zero.</div>

???
3 minutes. Exchangeable-label p≈.0062 using5000 shuffles and seed1104. Preserve outcomes and group counts; shuffle labels. Original blocks are absent, so this is an illustrative null model rather than an exact reconstruction of the trial randomization. The plus-one correction prevents p=0. Agreement with Welch is not independent replication.


---

class: balanced

# A result is more than a threshold

For the same two-sided Welch procedure:

The **95% interval excludes zero**, and **p < 0.05**.

That is a statistical conclusion under the procedure’s assumptions.

Report the estimate and interval alongside p. A larger p-value would not prove equality or no meaningful effect.

Different methods can yield different intervals or p-values.

<div class="student-note">Report the estimated size and uncertainty even when p is below 0.05; the threshold alone cannot show whether the result matters.</div>

???
3 minutes. The95% CI/test correspondence applies to compatible constructions for the same two-sided model. A bootstrap percentile interval and permutation p-value need not invert each other. Reporting a larger p does not prove equality. Tests block:3+3+3+3=12 minutes.


---

class: inverse, center, middle

# 4. Effect size and substantive importance



<div class="section-subtitle">Statistical evidence concerns uncertainty. Substantive importance requires context, units, costs, and a justified benchmark.</div>

???
Section transition included within its block timing.


---

class: balanced

# Size, precision and substantive importance

<div class="stat-strip">
  <div class="stat"><strong>1,794</strong>Mean contrast</div>
  <div class="stat"><strong>671</strong>Standard error</div>
  <div class="stat"><strong>474–3,115</strong>95% interval</div>
  <div class="stat"><strong>0.273</strong>Cohen’s d</div>
</div>

<div class="split">
  <div class="split-panel"><h2>Statistical evidence</h2><p>Two-sided Welch p = <strong>0.0079</strong></p><p>Observed sample: 185 training and 260 control participants.</p></div>
  <div class="split-panel alt"><h2>Substantive judgement</h2><p>Compare the estimate with a justified benchmark, programme costs, the price basis, and the research setting.</p></div>
</div>

<div class="result-band">Outcome: 1978 real earnings on the source-dollar scale. Report the estimate and uncertainty, not a software dump.</div>

<div class="student-note">The raw mean contrast answers 'how many source dollars?'; Cohen's d expresses the same gap relative to within-group variation.</div>

???
6 minutes. Cohen d=.273 scales the raw contrast by the pooled within-group SD; it does not impose equal variances on the Welch test. No universal d threshold determines policy importance. Historical source dollars cannot be read as current won. State design and assumptions around a compact result. N remains445 regardless of resampling count.


---

class: balanced

# Judgement challenge — pairs, 4 minutes

Suppose **2,000 source dollars** is an illustrative minimum worthwhile mean gain.

1. Is the estimated contrast above that benchmark?
2. Does the confidence interval establish a gain of at least 2,000?
3. What else would you need before judging programme value?

The benchmark is for discussion; it is not a measured programme cost.

<div class="student-note">An estimate can be close to a benchmark while the interval still includes values on both sides of it.</div>

???
2 minutes in pairs and2 for reporting. The point estimate is below2000, and the interval includes values below and above it; it does not establish a mean contrast of at least2000. Real valuation needs justified costs, price basis, horizon, distribution and applicability. Effect block:3+3+4=10 minutes.

# Methods follow the variables and design

<div class="evidence-list">
  <div class="evidence-row"><strong>Independent means</strong><span>Difference and Welch interval/test</span><span>Check units and independence</span></div>
  <div class="evidence-row"><strong>Repeated people</strong><span>Within-person differences</span><span>Pairing does not make change causal</span></div>
  <div class="evidence-row"><strong>Two numbers</strong><span>Scatterplot and Pearson/Spearman</span><span>Check shape, unusual values, dependence</span></div>
  <div class="evidence-row"><strong>Two proportions</strong><span>Counts and percentage-point gap</span><span>Check sample size and outcome definition</span></div>
</div>

<div class="caution">Repeated country-years and clusters need methods that respect dependence.</div>

<div class="student-note">Two datasets with similar columns may require different methods when observations are paired, clustered, weighted, or repeated over time.</div>

???
3 minutes. Repeated country-years are not independent new countries. Clustered records and survey weights may require different methods. A qualitative or descriptive final study should justify its evidence without being forced into a test.

class: balanced

# Two applications answer different questions

<div class="split">
  <div class="split-panel">
    <h2>Numerical association</h2>
    <p>Among 260 controls, compare baseline earnings in 1974 and 1975.</p>
    <p><strong>Pearson r = 0.675</strong><br><strong>Spearman ρ = 0.767</strong></p>
    <p>Inspect the shape, tied zeros, and unusual values before interpreting the association.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="split-panel alt">
    <h2>Binary outcome</h2>
    <p>Positive 1978 earnings: <strong>64.6%</strong> control and <strong>75.7%</strong> training.</p>
    <p><strong>Gap = 11.1 percentage points</strong><br>95% interval: 2.6 to 19.5 points.</p>
    <p>Positive earnings do not directly measure employment status.</p>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="caution">The association is observational. Dichotomizing earnings changes the question and discards information about earnings magnitude.</div>

<div class="student-note">Correlation retains earnings magnitude; a binary positive-earnings outcome asks a simpler question but discards how much people earned.</div>

???
4 minutes. Association within controls does not inherit a causal interpretation from training assignment. The scatterplot has tied zeros and high values; conventional Pearson inference assumptions may fit poorly. Binary counts are140/185 and168/260; the large-sample pooled-null z test gives p=.0127. Zero earnings do not establish unemployment. These applications answer different questions.

# Reference: the association plot

<div class="plot"><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Reference: the association plot" /></div>

.caption[Control participants, two pre-intervention earnings variables, n = 260.]

<div class="student-note">A positive pattern is visible, but tied zeros and high observations can affect correlation measures and their uncertainty.</div>

Reference only. The baseline scatterplot contains many zeros and high values. Pearson describes linear association; Spearman describes rank association. Neither identifies a training effect or causation from one earnings year to another.

<div class="plot"><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Reference: proportions and an interval" /></div>

.caption[Positive recorded earnings, not a directly verified employment rate.]

<div class="student-note">A percentage-point difference subtracts two proportions; it is different from a relative percentage increase.</div>

???
Reference only. Large-sample unpooled Wald95% interval2.57–19.55 points; pooled-null z p≈.01274. These approximations need adequate counts. The variable records positive earnings, not verified employment status.

class: balanced

# Reference: pairing and method assumptions

<div class="split">
  <div class="split-panel">
    <h2>Paired observations</h2>
    <p>When the same person supplies two measurements, analyse the <strong>within-person difference</strong>.</p>
    <p>The notebook compares 1975–1978 changes within each group. A before-after change alone does not identify the training effect.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="split-panel alt">
    <h2>Assumptions to check</h2>
    <p><strong>Welch:</strong> independent records and an appropriate mean target.</p>
    <p><strong>Bootstrap:</strong> resampling unit matches the design.</p>
    <p><strong>Permutation:</strong> labels are exchangeable under the null.</p>
    <p><strong>Association/proportions:</strong> dependence, shape, and counts support the method.</p>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="caution">A software function cannot validate the research design.</div>

<div class="student-note">Correct computation starts with the correct resampling or comparison unit: person, pair, cluster, or another design-defined unit.</div>

???
Reference only. Mean within-person change is about3288 for controls and4817 for training. Both paired tests are small-p, but neither change is the training effect by itself. Inspect the actual unit, dependence, selection, and measurement. Do not use independent-row methods for clusters or repeated country panels without justification. Checking assumptions is not a ritual of automatically running a normality test.

# Reference: a research-result checklist

A reader should find:

1. Question and study context
2. Quantity estimated and units
3. Observed sample and comparison
4. Estimate and uncertainty
5. Test result, if appropriate
6. Substantive interpretation and limitations

Report all relevant planned analyses and label exploratory work.

<div class="student-note">A reader should be able to reconstruct what was compared, what was estimated, and why the conclusion remains bounded.</div>

???
Reference only. Label exploratory work and report the analyses considered. Weak precision can still be informative. Never fabricate a finding or search seeds/specifications to achieve a preferred p-value.
